sections.overview: The Cigarette Beetle, called vrillette du tabac in French, is a cosmopolitan pest of stored tobacco and other dried products.
sections.identification: Adults are oval, reddish-brown beetles about two to three millimetres long. The head bends beneath the thorax, giving the beetle a humped outline.
sections.habitat: It occurs wherever dried tobacco is stored and also infests pantry foods, herbs, spices and dried flowers.
sections.diet: Larvae feed on dried commodities including tobacco, cereals, spices and dried fruit; adults do not feed, although they drink liquids.
sections.behavior: Adults hide in dark cracks and are most active at dusk and night; when disturbed, they may draw in their legs and remain still.
sections.reproduction: Females lay roughly ten to one hundred eggs in food, and development usually takes forty to ninety days depending on temperature and diet.
sections.ecology: It shares stored-product habitats with the related Drugstore Beetle, Stegobium paniceum, and the two are often confused. Serrated antennae and smooth, hairy wing cases help distinguish this species from that beetle’s clubbed antennae and striated wing cases.
sections.conservation: Penn State describes it as a common stored-product pest in Pennsylvania, especially of dried herbs, spices and flowers.
